title: He, this, that, who
goal: Point to people and things with three demonstratives, use third-person pronouns, and join two sentences with a qui clause.
bekal: tell *hic* (this, near me) from *ille* (that, far away)
build *qui* clauses with the right form

dialogs.title: Colloquium — In foro, ante tabernam
dialogs.intro: Quintus's family runs into people — not all of whom they know.

notes: **Hic, ille, is — three different distances.** *Hic* points to what is near the speaker ("this"), *ille* to what is far away ("that, over there"), and *is* to what has already been mentioned ("he, the one just named"). English uses "this", "that", and "he/she/it" for the same distinctions.

**Eius means "his/her/its", belonging to someone else.** Look at *taberna eius* ("his shop") and *uxor eius* ("his wife"). *Eius* never changes its ending — one form for masculine, feminine, and neuter. It differs from *suus*, which is used when the owner is the subject of the sentence itself.

**Puer quem vidi — the linking word takes its form from its own clause.** *Quem* is in the object form because inside the clause it is the object of *vidi*. Its gender and number come from *puer*, but its job comes from its own clause. This two-source rule is the heart of the whole unit.
**Ipsa vidi — "I saw it myself".** *Ipse, ipsa, ipsum* means "self" and is used for emphasis. Iulia is female, so she says *ipsa*. This word gives the phrase *ipso facto* — "by the act itself".

blocks.text: All three change endings like adjectives, but they share two special endings: the "of" form ends in *-ius* and the "to" form in *-i*. Learn those two endings once, and all three become easy.

head: Job
is, ea, id (he, the one mentioned)
hic, haec, hoc (this)
ille, illa, illud (that)

blocks.text: All three can stand alone ("that one", "he") or go with a noun ("that man"). *Ille vir* means "that man"; *ille* by itself means "he over there". The form is the same either way.

blocks.title: Their traces in modern languages
items: *ille* gave French its article *le*, Italian *il*, and Spanish *el*. Latin had no articles; its daughters made them from this demonstrative.
*ipse* gave us *ipso facto* and *ipse dixit* ("he said it himself").
*idem, eadem, idem* means "the same", and is still used in footnotes as *ibid.* and *id.*
*hic et nunc* — "here and now" — uses *hic* in its sense of place, not "this".

sections.title: The linking word qui, quae, quod

blocks.text: A "who/which …" clause is joined with *qui*. Its form comes from two places at once, and that is the only thing that needs practice.

head: Sentence
Translation
Why it has that form
rows: The boy who is coming is my friend.
masculine singular from *puer*; subject because he does the coming
The boy whom I saw is my friend.
masculine singular from *puer*; object because he is the one seen
The girl whose book I'm reading …
feminine singular; "of" because it's her book
The friend to whom I sent a letter …
masculine singular; "to" because he receives it
The dinner you're making is the best.
feminine singular from *cena*; object in its clause
The soldiers who guard the city are brave.
masculine plural; subject in its clause

blocks.text: How to check: cover the main sentence and ask, "inside this clause, is it doing the action or receiving it?" The answer decides the form. Gender and number are simply copied from the word it describes.
*Qui* can also stand without a word to describe, meaning "the one who": *qui vult, potest* — "the one who wants, can". Its neuter means "what": *quod dicis verum est* — "what you say is true".
The question words *quis* and *quid* use almost the same table as *qui*, and you have been using some of their forms since Unit 1.

head: Job
Person
Thing
Example
rows: Quem vides? — Who do you see?
Cuius liber est? — Whose book is this?
Cui scribis? — Who are you writing to?
Cum quo ambulas? — Who are you walking with?

blocks.text: Notice that almost every Latin question word starts with *qu-*. That's no accident: English has the same pattern with *wh-*, and both inherited it from the same parent language, thousands of years before Rome was founded.
